claims.text: The initial non-equilibrium Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy has a metastable, predominantly solid-solution microstructure with only minor secondary phases.
High-temperature and corrosive exposure transforms the metastable solid solution into a phase-separated structure.
The phase-separated structure contains stable Mg-rich intermetallic compounds.
Segregation of Mg and other constituent elements under thermal and corrosive stress promotes nucleation and growth of stable intermetallic phases.
Mg-rich intermetallic phases interrupt the continuity and homogeneity of the passive oxide scale.
Disruption of the passive oxide scale diminishes protection against high-temperature oxidation.
The evolved intermetallic-containing microstructure modifies corrosion kinetics, possibly through localized galvanic effects.
Relative to the untreated metastable baseline, thermally and chemically exposed samples will contain distinct Mg-rich intermetallics.
Relative to the untreated baseline, evolved samples will form a less protective high-temperature oxide scale.
Relative to the untreated baseline, evolved samples will exhibit increased localized corrosion rates.
Rapid cooling can be used to retain the alloy in a metastable, nominally single-phase state.
A thermal treatment can be designed to promote intermetallic phase formation in the alloy.

The proposed mechanism is intended to apply to Mg-containing high-entropy alloys with densities below 6 g/cm3 and alloying-element contrasts that permit both metastable solid solutions and stable intermetallic states.
Al, Cu, Zn, and Gd are examples of contrasting alloying elements within the proposed applicability boundary.
